title: Equilibrium and Acid–Base Chemistry
description: How far reactions go, how to calculate it, and what that means for solubility, pH and buffers.

entries.name: The equilibrium constant
entries.tagline: A number that says how far a reaction goes before it settles.

sections.text: For a reversible reaction aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD at equilibrium, the ratio of product to reactant concentrations, each raised to its coefficient, is constant at a given temperature.
For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ this gives Kc = [NH₃]² ÷ ([N₂][H₂]³).

points: Pure solids and pure liquids are left out of the expression, because their concentrations do not change.
K much bigger than 1 means products are favored. K much smaller than 1 means reactants are favored.
K changes only with temperature. Changing concentrations or pressure shifts the position of equilibrium, but not K.
Kp uses partial pressures of gases. Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, where Δn is the change in moles of gas.
Reversing a reaction gives 1/K. Multiplying the equation by n raises K to the power n. Adding reactions multiplies their K values.

quiz.q: Which of these is left out of an equilibrium constant expression?
What can change the value of K?

entries.name: The reaction quotient
entries.tagline: Compare Q with K to see which way a mixture will move.

sections.text: The reaction quotient Q has the same form as K but uses the concentrations at any moment, not just at equilibrium.

facts: Too many reactants. The reaction moves forward, toward the products.
Too many products. The reaction moves in reverse.

sections.text: If K = 4.0 and the mixture currently has Q = 1.0, then Q < K, so the reaction proceeds forward until Q rises to 4.0.

quiz.q: If Q is greater than K, which way does the reaction move?

entries.name: ICE tables
entries.tagline: A tidy way to find equilibrium concentrations.

sections.text: An ICE table has three rows: Initial concentrations, Change, and Equilibrium concentrations. Use the coefficients to write the changes in terms of one unknown x.

points: Start with 1.00 M H₂ and 1.00 M I₂ and no HI.
Change: H₂ −x, I₂ −x, HI +2x. Equilibrium: [H₂] = [I₂] = 1.00 − x and [HI] = 2x.
K = (2x)² ÷ (1.00 − x)² = 50. Taking the square root: 2x ÷ (1.00 − x) = 7.07.
Solving gives x = 0.779. So [HI] = 1.56 M and [H₂] = [I₂] = 0.22 M.

sections.text: If K is very small, x is tiny compared with the starting concentration, so 1.00 − x can be treated as 1.00. Check afterwards that x is below about 5% of the starting value.

quiz.q: What do the letters in an ICE table stand for?

entries.name: Solubility product and the common ion effect
entries.tagline: The equilibrium constant for a slightly soluble salt dissolving.

sections.text: For a salt that dissolves only a little, the dissolving reaction reaches equilibrium. The equilibrium constant is the solubility product, Ksp.

points: If s is the amount that dissolves, [Ag⁺] = [Cl⁻] = s, so s² = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ and s = 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ mol/L.
For a salt such as CaF₂ = Ca²⁺ + 2F⁻, Ksp = [Ca²⁺][F⁻]² = s(2s)² = 4s³.

sections.text: Adding an ion that is already in the equilibrium makes the salt less soluble. In 0.10 M NaCl, the solubility of AgCl falls to Ksp ÷ 0.10 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ mol/L.
Calculate Q from the mixed concentrations. If Q is greater than Ksp, a precipitate forms until Q falls to Ksp.

quiz.q: What happens to the solubility of AgCl when NaCl is added to the solution?

entries.name: Strong and weak acids and bases
entries.tagline: Strong acids dissociate completely, and weak acids only partly.

sections.text: A strong acid dissociates completely in water. The common ones are HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, H₂SO₄ (first hydrogen only) and HClO₄. A weak acid, such as acetic acid, dissociates only slightly, and an equilibrium is set up.
A smaller Ka means a weaker acid. pKa = −log Ka, so a smaller pKa means a stronger acid.

points: Acetic acid has Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, so pKa = 4.74.
For a conjugate acid–base pair, Ka × Kb = Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C, so pKa + pKb = 14.
The conjugate base of a weak acid is a weak base. The conjugate base of a strong acid is too weak to matter.
Strong bases include the hydroxides of group 1 and the heavier group 2 metals. Ammonia is a common weak base.

quiz.q: For a conjugate acid–base pair in water at 25 °C, pKa + pKb equals…

entries.name: pH calculations
entries.tagline: Turning concentrations into pH and back.

sections.text: The last two hold at 25 °C. Water itself ionizes slightly, which is why Kw exists. In water, H⁺ is really H₃O⁺, the hydronium ion.
A 0.0010 M HCl solution is fully dissociated, so [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ and pH = 3.00.

points: Each pH unit is a factor of 10 in [H⁺].
At 25 °C, neutral water has pH 7.00. The neutral pH shifts slightly with temperature because Kw does.

quiz.q: What is the pH of 0.0010 M HCl?

entries.name: Buffers and the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation
entries.tagline: Solutions that resist changes in pH.

sections.text: A buffer is a mixture of a weak acid and its conjugate base (or a weak base and its conjugate acid). Added acid is used up by the base, and added base is used up by the acid, so the pH changes only a little.
This is the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation.

points: When [A⁻] = [HA], the pH equals the pKa. An acetate buffer with equal amounts has pH 4.74.
A buffer works best within about 1 pH unit of its pKa, and its capacity depends on how much acid and base it holds.
Blood is buffered at about pH 7.4 mainly by carbonic acid and hydrogen carbonate.
Calibrating a pH meter uses buffer solutions of known pH.

quiz.q: In a buffer, when [A⁻] equals [HA], the pH is…

entries.name: Titration curves
entries.tagline: A graph of pH against the volume of titrant added.

sections.text: The pH changes slowly at first, then very sharply near the equivalence point, then slowly again. The middle of the steep part is the equivalence point.

facts: Starts at low pH, equivalence at pH 7.
Starts higher, equivalence above 7 because the conjugate base is basic. A buffer region appears before it.

points: At the half-equivalence point of a weak acid, half the acid has become its conjugate base, so [A⁻] = [HA] and pH = pKa. This is a way to measure pKa.
Choose an indicator that changes color near the pH of the equivalence point. Phenolphthalein (about pH 8–10) suits a weak acid with a strong base.

quiz.q: At the half-equivalence point in the titration of a weak acid, the pH equals…

entries.name: Acid–base definitions
entries.tagline: Three increasingly general ways to say what an acid is.

facts: An acid makes H⁺ in water. A base makes OH⁻ in water.
An acid donates a proton (H⁺). A base accepts a proton.
An acid accepts an electron pair. A base donates an electron pair.

sections.text: When an acid donates a proton, what is left is its conjugate base. In HCl + H₂O → Cl⁻ + H₃O⁺, Cl⁻ is the conjugate base of HCl, and H₃O⁺ is the conjugate acid of H₂O.
Boron trifluoride has an empty orbital and accepts the lone pair from ammonia. BF₃ is a Lewis acid even though it has no H⁺ to give.
A substance that can act as an acid or a base is amphoteric. Water and hydrogen carbonate (HCO₃⁻) are examples.
